bp: An online ad system has to decide, in the moment after a user request, which ads deserve high positions. Older post-click models often ask a yes-or-no question: after someone clicks, will they eventually convert? This paper studies a harder business question: after the click, how much money will the following purchases add up to? That amount is gross merchandise volume, or GMV, and it matters because two clicks that both convert can still have very different value. One user may buy one low-priced item; another may return several times and buy more. The paper serves ad ranking systems that must estimate this future monetary value while the future is still unfinished. Its contribution begins with TRACE, a benchmark built from complete transaction sequences after each click, so delayed value can be studied as a stream rather than as a frozen table.
wh: The hard part is that the answer is both late and numerical. In conversion-rate prediction, a delayed label is usually a delayed yes or no. For GMV, the label is a changing amount, and one click can produce several later purchases whose sum becomes the final value. A model trained too early sees only a partial receipt and may learn that the click was worth less than it really was. The abstract says the GMV label distribution evolves rapidly, so the meaning of recent examples can change while training continues online. It also says repurchase samples have a substantially different label distribution from single-purchase samples. That means the system is not just missing labels; it is mixing two different behavior patterns under one target. The central tension is speed versus completeness: ad ranking needs fast learning from recent data, but the monetary truth arrives slowly and unevenly.
naive: A smart beginner might reuse the delayed-feedback machinery from conversion-rate prediction. Treat each click as an example, wait for purchases to appear, attach the observed GMV as the label, and train one regression model to predict that number from click and user-ad features. If a label is incomplete, simply train on the money seen so far or wait longer before using the example. This breaks in two ways described by the paper. Training on seen-so-far money teaches systematic under-estimation because later purchases are missing. Waiting longer makes the model stale in a setting where the GMV distribution changes quickly. A single model also blurs single-purchase and repurchase cases, even though the benchmark analysis finds that their label distributions differ substantially.
ap: The paper's core move is to stop pretending that all post-click value follows one shape. It builds TRACE so the whole purchase sequence after a click is visible and usable in online streaming training. From that evidence, it proposes READER, a repurchase-aware dual-branch predictor. In plain terms, the model first asks which kind of path the click seems likely to follow: a one-purchase path or a repurchase path. A routing component makes that repurchase prediction and selectively activates the expert parameters suited to that case. The amount prediction is then handled by the branch whose training signal better matches the expected behavior pattern. READER also changes the training target dynamically, calibrating the observed amount so incomplete labels do not push the model toward values that are too small simply because the later transactions have not arrived yet.
mech: The mechanism starts with a click and the transaction sequence that later rises from that click. TRACE stores this sequence, so the training process can see not only whether a purchase happened but also how purchase amounts accumulate over time. In an online streaming setting, examples arrive and labels mature while the model is being updated. For each training case, the system must represent the click context and the currently available post-click evidence, then predict whether this click belongs to the repurchase-like group or the single-purchase-like group. That prediction is used by a router. The router does not merely add a label; it controls which expert parameters are used for the GMV estimate. One branch can specialize in cases where the final value mostly comes from one purchase, while the other can specialize in cases where value is accumulated across several purchases. The model then outputs a numerical GMV prediction, not just a purchase probability. During training, the regression target is dynamically calibrated: if the currently observed GMV is likely incomplete because delayed purchases have not all arrived, the target is adjusted to reduce the under-estimation that would come from treating the partial sum as final. The output is a value estimate usable by ad ranking.
math: The main mathematics is estimation under delayed, partial observation. The unknown quantity is a final sum of money after a click. At any training time, the model may see only part of that sum, so it must learn from a censored receipt: useful, but not complete. Regression is the act of predicting a number by choosing model settings that make predicted amounts close to observed target amounts. Here, that target itself is unstable, so the paper adds calibration: a correction that changes the target used for learning when the observed amount is likely too low. The second mathematical idea is mixture modeling through routing. Instead of forcing one set of settings to fit all clicks, the router estimates which subpopulation the click resembles, then activates an expert branch. This is a way of saying that different cases may obey different value patterns. The tradeoff is specialization versus routing error. Separate branches can fit single-purchase and repurchase distributions more cleanly, but only if the router's repurchase prediction is informative. The benchmark also brings sequence thinking: purchases after a click form an ordered trail whose accumulated total changes as time passes.
dots: This paper sits at the intersection of ad ranking, e-commerce recommendation, delayed feedback, and online learning. It connects to conversion-rate prediction because both ask what a click eventually means, but it moves from a yes-or-no outcome to a continuously growing money amount. It connects to ranking because the prediction is meant to guide which ads get better positions, where an under-valued repurchase click could be ranked too low. It also connects to broader conference work on distribution change: the abstract says the GMV label distribution evolves rapidly, so yesterday's completed examples may not describe today's stream well. A nearby e-commerce idea in the repo is fine-grained CVR modeling, where the system must avoid treating all item or price situations alike. READER makes a related move for post-click value: split cases whose outcome distributions differ instead of averaging them into one noisy target.
ww: The method should help because it aligns the model's training problem with the actual shape of the business event. If final GMV is an accumulated sequence, then early partial labels are biased downward. Dynamic target calibration directly attacks that bias by preventing the model from learning that unfinished receipts are complete receipts. If repurchase and single-purchase clicks have different label distributions, then a single predictor is forced to compromise. It may learn an average rule that is too high for ordinary one-purchase cases and too low for repeated-purchase cases. A router with two expert branches gives the model a controlled way to use different rules for different paths. This is not magic extra information; it works only because the benchmark analysis found a real split in the data. The causal intuition is simple: when two kinds of customer behavior generate money in different ways, first sort the behavior type, then estimate value within the right type.
po: The payoff is a more faithful target for online advertisement ranking. TRACE gives researchers a benchmark where delayed GMV can be studied with complete transaction sequences rather than improvised labels. READER gives the ranking model a way to distinguish clicks that may lead to repeated purchases from clicks that likely end after one purchase, and to train without treating incomplete GMV as the final truth. Grounded in the abstract, the practical gain is reduced under-estimation and better post-click GMV prediction in streaming ad systems where the objective is moving from conversion probability toward monetary value.
limits: The abstract supports the mechanism but does not prove every deployment condition. READER depends on the repurchase router being good enough; if repurchase predictions are noisy, examples may be sent to the wrong branch. Dynamic calibration also assumes the model can estimate how incomplete a current label is from available evidence. TRACE contains complete transaction sequences from each click, so systems without comparable logging may not reproduce the setup. The paper's claims are about post-click GMV prediction, not all forms of ad value, user welfare, or advertiser profit. It also separates repurchase and single-purchase samples, but the abstract does not show whether two branches are enough for all product categories, user segments, or seasonal shifts.
